title: Several experiments, one hierarchical mean
dek: When each site is noisy, a shared distribution over site effects is the scientific model. The famous eight-schools picture is this geometry — here with original district-survey numbers, not a textbook table.
story: Eight labs, eight districts, eight trials: each reports an estimated effect yⱼ with a standard error σⱼ that you are, for a moment, willing to treat as known. The no-pooling picture treats the eight numbers as eight unrelated truths. The complete-pooling picture pretends they were one experiment. Both are usually wrong.

Hierarchical model: yⱼ | θⱼ ~ N(θⱼ, σⱼ²), θⱼ ~ N(μ, τ²). The posterior (or BLUP) of θⱼ shrinks yⱼ toward μ by an amount that depends on σⱼ versus τ. A tiny noisy site moves a lot; a precise site keeps its identity. That is the whole visual.

τ is not a nuisance to profile into oblivion without comment. If τ is near 0, you almost complete-pool and should say the sites look exchangeable. If τ is large, you almost no-pool and the shared mean is a weak story. Estimating τ from eight noisy sites is itself noisy — show p(τ | y), not a starred test that τ = 0.
deepTitle: The model, and what this is not
deep: Known-σⱼ Normal is a teaching likelihood. In a real survey, σⱼ comes from a first-stage model (binomial, sandwich, design-based). Plugging in σ̂ⱼ ignores that uncertainty; a fully Bayesian stack would put a model on the raw rows. Use the two-stage version when that is all you were given in a table.

The geometry is not a licence to average incompatible estimands. Eight “effects” that are actually different scientific functionals (different endpoints, different controls) should not share θⱼ ~ N(μ, τ²). Exchangeability is a scientific claim.
A forest plot of no-pooling intervals plus a hierarchical diamond is the usual figure. The diamond is not an LRT. The shrunk site intervals are the ones that should appear on a map of districts.

This plate deliberately does not reproduce any copyrighted school-coaching table. The algebra is older than any one book. If you want a historical pointer, look up hierarchical Normal models in a library; do not paste them here.

formulas.label: Two-stage hierarchical Normal
formulas.expression: yⱼ | θⱼ ~ N(θⱼ, σⱼ²),   θⱼ ~ N(μ, τ²)
formulas.note: σⱼ treated as known in the teaching version.

formulas.label: Shrinkage toward μ
formulas.expression: E[θⱼ | y, μ, τ] = Bⱼ μ + (1−Bⱼ) yⱼ,   Bⱼ = σⱼ² / (σⱼ² + τ²)
formulas.note: Bⱼ is the weight on the shared mean — large when site j is noisy.

visual.caption: Eight schematic site estimates (bars at no-pool yⱼ) versus shrunk θ̃ⱼ sitting closer to a shared μ (the flatter set). Noisy sites move more. This is the multi-experiment idea, drawn with invented district SEs — not a reproduced coaching-study table.

example.title: Eight district log-odds, invented SEs
example.setup: District log-odds of FQ-R among RR-TB, two-stage: y = (0.1, 0.4, −0.2, 0.8, 0.0, 0.3, 1.1, −0.5) with σ = (0.5, 0.45, 0.6, 0.25, 0.7, 0.4, 0.2, 0.55). These numbers are original teaching values.

steps.title: No pooling
steps.body: District 7 looks high (1.1, se 0.2). District 8 looks low (−0.5, se 0.55). A map of yⱼ will advertise 8 as “protective” and 7 as an outbreak — one of those SEs is a fog.

steps.title: Fit τ, μ
steps.body: A method-of-moments or Bayes fit will put μ somewhere near the precision-weighted mean and τ modest. District 8 shrinks hard toward μ because σ₈ is large. District 7 barely moves.

steps.title: Sentence in the paper
steps.body: “District-specific log-odds are shrunk toward a survey mean; the apparent low district is compatible with noise.” That sentence is the eight-experiments idea. It does not require anyone’s table of schools.

example.takeaway: Several noisy experiments: shrink in proportion to their σⱼ² relative to τ². Draw p(τ|y). Do not photocopy a famous table to do it.

check.prompt: In E[θⱼ|y] = Bⱼ μ + (1−Bⱼ) yⱼ with Bⱼ = σⱼ²/(σⱼ²+τ²), a very large site-SE σⱼ means:
check.why: Noisy yⱼ gets little weight. B is the weight on μ in this parameterisation.

whyWrong.τ² must be infinite: τ is shared, not set by one σⱼ.

check.prompt: σⱼ² = 4, τ² = 1, yⱼ = 10, μ = 2. Shrunk mean Bμ + (1−B)y with B = 4/(4+1) equals:
check.why: B = 0.8, 0.8×2 + 0.2×10 = 1.6 + 2 = 3.6. The noisy 10 is pulled most of the way to 2.

whyWrong.8.4: If you swapped B and 1−B: 0.2×2 + 0.8×10 = 8.4 — the wrong weight on μ.
